# Copper May 2012 - The old adage of “sell in May and go away” seems to be holding true again this year. The impetus behind the decline in copper prices has been the resurgence of the Euro crisis and the Greek situation in particular. The sell off has been further compounded by long liquidation during the month on both the LME and Comex. Interest for material is increasingly subdued across Europe and the USA, while the negative arbitrage between SHFE and the LME has kept Chinese buyers out of the market. - We remain of the opinion that copper prices are likely to pick up during the second half of this year, reflecting a general improvement in market sentiment, most notably in China. History has shown that market sentiment has been far more responsive to Chinese metal trade data than to changes in underlying demand so we are unlikely to see any uplift in price until Chinese inventories begin to be drawn down and imports pick up. - Chinese consumption disappointed badly on the downside in April and there is every indication that May could prove to be as poor. Elsewhere in Asia there are some more encouraging signs to report with Japan, South Korea and Taiwan all recording sequential growth in semis output from January to March and possibly into April. US consumption is making some gains from a low base but progress is uneven with April rod output falling on the low side of expectations. Europe remains a concern with the German automobile sector the only stand out performer. - In a quiet concentrates market during May, representative spot selling terms between miners and traders trended flat to lower in comparison with last month’s levels. With Chinese smelters having secured an increased proportion of their concentrate requirements under long-term contracts this year, the continued unfavourable TCRCs, negative arbitrage between the SHFE and LME copper prices and weak order books have seen any spot buying activity limited to ‘hand to mouth’ requirements. Under these conditions, buying terms strengthened slightly with figures in the range $40/t & 4.0c/lb to $45/t & 4.5c/lb achieved depending on quality and shipping period. Elsewhere, spot prices in India are understood to have remained at similar levels to last month, in the mid 40s and 4s. #### **Copper key forecasts** ||**2011**|**%**|**2012**|**%**|**2013**|**%**|**2014**|**%**| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |**Global (kt)**||||||||| |Total Mine Production|16245|0.4|16975|4.5|18701|10.2|19661|5.1| |Total Smelter Production|15431|4.5|15893|3.0|17320|9.0|18197|5.1| |Refined Production|19684|3.7|20259|2.9|21955|8.4|23066|5.1| |Consumption|19806|2.6|20437|3.2|21386|4.6|22580|5.6| |Concentrate Market Balance|-304||0||100||100|| |Metal Market Balance|-122||-178||569||486|| |MetalStocks- Days ofCons|52||47||54||59|| |**Prices**||||||||| |Cash LME Price ($/t)|8810||8477||8150||7825|| |(c/lb)|400||385||

Prices have once again been swept along and downwards by the deteriorating economic news, further dampened by an ongoing appreciation in the US dollar. Interest for material is increasingly subdued across Europe and the USA, while the negative arbitrage between SHFE and the LME has kept Chinese buyers out of the market. Copper prices came under pressure amid the ongoing dithering by the Euro zone’s leadership over the sovereign debt crisis which led to a broader sell off across the LME metals last week. Three-month copper prices traded to lows of $7,530/t on the 23rd May, close to levels last seen in January this year. The sell off has been further compounded by long liquidation during the month on both the LME and Comex. The latest available data from the CFTC indicates that money managers have exited the metal, with copper switching to a net short position for the first time since January, further underscoring the dim short-term view for the red metal. #### **CFTC copper positions** '000 Contracts

**A new ETF** Ironically the decline in copper prices has come around the same time as JPMorgan announced a copper ETF. JP Morgan filed plans to list its fund (JPM XF Physical Copper Trust) on the NYSE Euronext exchange as early as June this year. This comes almost two years after both JPMorgan and Blackrock first announced their intentions to create physical copper funds. For now it remains to be seen how much interest JPMorgan’s investment vehicle will attract other than the reactions from both Red Kite and Southwire that this type of fund would inflate prices and squeeze supply by removing as much as a third of the London Metal Exchange's copper stocks. The only other physically backed ETF is currently on offer from ETF Securities with currently 2.126kt allocated against it, with a maximum of just 6.882kt (in April 2012) since its introduction in December 2012. If fully subscribed, the 60kt ETF would represent just 0.3% of annual production and as this material is expected to be built up slowly, it seems unlikely that it will have much impact on price. Moreover, at a time when China is entering into a period of slower growth and with many new copper mine projects under development, there would seem far less upside potential to copper prices. On this basis

, one might expect there to be even less incentive for investors to buy into another copper ETF. **A squeeze unravelled** Meanwhile the Euro crisis has overshadowed the unravelling of the squeeze that we discussed in our publication last month. At the end of April cancelled warrants on the LME had tipped 42% of the 256.40kt stocks on the LME. By the 14th May, a week before the crisis hit, cancelled warrants had fallen to just 20% of the total 215.35kt stocks on the LME. It comes as no surprise that over this time frame the cash to 3-months backwardation that had flared out to over $150/t at the end of April, had narrowed to just $25/t by 15th May (and down from $129/t the previous day). This sharp decline came at the same time as the LME’s warrant banding report indicated that no single position in copper controlled at least 30% of stockpiles as of 14th May. Up until the 11th May there had been a dominant position of between 50-79% of LME warrants, which has now been wound down. **Cloudy outlook adds to consumer woes** The ongoing economic uncertainty is affecting downstream consumer confidence across Northern Europe. Our discussions with downstream copper consumers indicate that orders have been slowing since April and expectations for June are no different. With limited visibility, semis manufacturers are living hand-to-mouth. We understand that spot enquiries are coming through in Europe, although these are for small volumes and are reflective of requirements due to late shipments rather than a need to add to volumes. This is disappointing given that Q2 is usually the seasonally stronger period for copper consumption. However it is not surprising as we understand that consumers locked in sufficient quantities under contract with producers amid an unsettled macro economic and another perceived tight year for cathode. Moreover scrap flows have been better than many had anticipated and we understand that some fabricators have been able to consume additional scrap units. What is clear is that the ebb and flow of scrap remains closely correlated to movements in copper and as metal prices began to slide through May, scrap was less readily available. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

**Premiums hold steady in Europe but tick higher in the USA and China** Premiums are stable in Europe, reportedly at around the $80/t level, supported by low and declining LME stocks in the region. That said, if consumers need material they are willing to pay slightly higher premia for prompt delivery. One light at the end of the tunnel in an otherwise lacklustre European market is the automotive sector, with demand holding up well despite the nervousness across the other market areas in Europe. We understand that there have even been some requests for advance Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2012 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update shipments from this sector. Meanwhile the premium for imported copper into China was reported to be in a wider range of $30-70/t compared to the $20-60/t range at the beginning of May. Cathode premiums have moved up again this month and are currently being quoted in the 5.5-7c/lb range on both a delivered Midwest and East Coast basis. These higher levels are being supported by the maintenance closure at Kennecott and elevated freight rates due to higher fuel costs and a tight trucking market. **China is the key** While from an economic perspective, Europe remains very much in the limelight, it is China that is key to this copper market. That country’s general lack of activity remains a concern. Where many had anticipated a strong pick up in Chinese activity in Q2, we have maintained the view that China would only come back into the market in (full) force over the second half of the year. A combination of declining levels of inventories and the SHFE/LME arbitrage will dictate to what extent and when China will return to the international market with any renewed vigour. In the interim, the continued decline of China’s manufacturing sector is adding to the uncertainty in the market. HSBC’s Flash China Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index for May fell to 48.7 from 49.3 the previous month which is the seventh consecutive month that the PPI came in below 50. That said it is unlikely that China’s leaders will simply sit back and watch the economy fall further. Beijing policy makers have already made some announcements that should boost liquidity, public housing and infrastructure investment and consumption. Once these measures start to filter through, we expect China to come back into the market in earnest, as domestic stocks are consumed. Despite China’s importance to this market, the data sets available only add obscurity to what is an already opaque market, hindering rather than aiding our understanding of the real state of demand and the current level of inventories. Copper imports into China have remained high since the last quarter of 2011. This had been taken initially as a bullish sign, but as it became clearer that a large proportion of this metal was delivered into inventory it began to weigh on se

ntiment.  While all market observers have their own take of what the real level of inventories are in China, the reality is that no-one really knows how much is held by the SRB or in bonded warehouses and if, or indeed when any of this material might be released into what is clearly an overstocked market.  We know that at the end of April several large Chinese copper smelters including Jiangxi Copper announced their intention to deliver refined copper cathodes to the London Metal Exchange warehouses over the coming months in an effort to boost the availability of copper in the global market.  So far only 23.1kt of copper has been delivered into LME Asian warehouses since the end of April.  In the absence of trade data it is impossible to know at this time if these are diverted shipments or exports out of China.  We would suspect the former rather than latter given the VAT losses on Chinese exports. 

Meanwhile data on semis output of China suggests a 22% increase over the first four months of the year.  This does not reconcile with our discussions with market participants and would also suggest that inventory reportedly built over the tail end of 2011 should have been drawn down over the same period given that refined production over that timeframe grew by 6.9%.  Moreover, scrap trade figures lead to more questions than answers as it is impossible to determine a) the copper content, b) the difference in unit value between what China reports compared to what is reported by those exporting countries and finally the difference in the incoming tonnages reported by China when compared to the volume of scrap from the exporting countries. 

What is clear is that the outlook for the copper market and price support will be determined by China.  If, as we believe, the semis data is suspect at best and that the actual volumes of scrap imports are inflated (best not step into the debate over copper content issues), we remain bullish that China will be back in H2 2012.  There are also some positive signs emerging; discussions we have had suggest that stocks in bonded warehouse are being drawn down from the high levels while reported inventories at SHFE warehouses have maintained a declining trend since peaking at just over 222kt in early April.  And in the meantime the SHFE/LME arbitrage, while still negative has come in to ~$200/t from over $600/t at the end of April. 

**Economic indicators dampen market sentiment** With little comfort offered from the macro economic outlook and a demand side picture that is showing signs of stagnating, there is no incentive for any build of inventory through the consumption chain.  Even a weaker set of output data from some producers has failed to support.  Meanwhile, the shortterm technical indicators show that copper and the Euro are very closely correlated, suggesting that some traders’ models have linked the two electronically.  If this is the case the view is that when the Euro breaks 1.26, copper will breach $7500/t.

We would expect the Chinese to come back to the market if prices tumble below $7000/t, but for now copper remains volatile. We remain of the opinion that copper prices are likely to pick up during the second half of this year, reflecting a general improvement in market sentiment, most notably in China. However, we still feel that any uplift in price is unlikely to fully reflect the turnaround in China’s fortunes, primarily due to the elevated levels of cathode imports since Q4 2011 that have contributed to the large increase in inventories since late last year. This means that as Chinese copper demand picks up, much of this will be satisfied from domestic stocks, at least initially and not from heightened metal imports. History has shown that market sentiment has been far more responsive to Chinese metal trade data than to changes in underlying demand, the latter being far harder to quantify. ### **Europe** 

**European demand slows in Q2** After a reasonable opening quarter, Western European copper demand has lost some momentum through the opening months of the second quarter.  Prevailing economic and political tensions have contributed to the uncertainty as have weaker copper prices.  Visibility is very low and order books are slim as customers are unwilling to commit themselves beyond their own limited horizons.  Mills report no difficulties in securing supplies of refined metal or scrap and spot premiums for grade A cathode have dipped to $80/t as buying interest has dwindled. 

**Germany stands strong alone** Although Germany remains by far the best performing national market within Western Europe; there are nevertheless some pockets of weakness emerging for the German semis industry.  This is not surprising as typically some 75-80% of German semis exports are destined for Western or Eastern European markets. Aurubis reported wire rod production of 179kt CYQ1 2012 up 15% from CYQ4 2011, but down 10% from CYQ1 2011.  Its output of refinery shapes for the brass mill sector exhibited a similar trend, rising 27% sequentially to 47kt in CYQ1 2012, but falling 15% year-on-year.  Production of flat rolled and speciality products expanded to 60kt increasing both sequentially and year-on-year due to its acquisition of Luvata’s flat rolled assets. 

**German end use industries remain optimistic** According to the German Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers Association (ZVEI) the electrical appliance industry’s sales increased by nearly 4% in the first two months of 2012 while its output rose by over 5%.  The automobile industry is the real strength behind Germany’s performance.  The President of the VDA recently said, “The German market is in a robust mood, but the high fuel prices are putting the brakes on sales of new cars.  The additional costs at the fuel pumps are holding back consumer spending.”  While European new vehicle registrations fell 7% year-on-year to 4.5 million units in Jan-Apr 2012, German registrations rose 3%.  German vehicle output was flat in the first quarter, maintaining the very strong level of 1.5 million units achieved in Q1 2011. Export volumes are also stable but do stand to gain later this year from a growing recovery in new car registrations in China, which rose by a healthy 14% year-on-year in April.  One in five cars sold in China is German while four out of every five premium cars sold in China is also German.  The strong automotive components sector drove sales at Nuremburg headquar

tered cablemaker Leoni to a record €969m in Q1 2012, led by a 14% surge in wiring harness revenues, despite lower copper prices. #### **Italian semis production – (kt)** 40 360

**Rod markets soften in the Rest of Europe** Outside of Germany rod demand has softened a little. Sales continue to hold up better in Northern Europe than in the South, although even the former mills have been struggling as exceptionally keenly priced Russian rod has gained some market share in Scandinavia. Finland, Sweden and Norway Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2012 Page 6 of 21 Copper Monthly Update saw the only growth in rod consumption in Q1 led by strong power cable orders for submarine and offshore wind energy projects. Q1 consumption fell by 7% year-on-year in the UK and by 12% in Denmark despite improving demand from the construction sector. However, Italian consumption dropped by 12-13% after an 8% contraction in local rod production in Q1 2012. A sharp deceleration in enamelled wire production, due to weaker orders from the home appliance and automotive components industry, was largely to blame with Italian winding wire specialist IRCE reporting a 27% year-onyear drop in Q1 sales to €100m. As LME quarterly copper prices fell by only 10% year-on-year in this period this underlines the apparent decrease in volumes. However, the company was still predicting an upturn in its enamelled wire volumes in the second half of the current year. Outside of Northern Europe, utility power cable order volumes were slowing due to the timing of certain projects. **Prysmian wields the axe** Prysmian’s acquisition of Draka over a year ago resulted in a global review of the combined group’s operational manufacturing footprint and headcount to identify the synergy savings necessary to justify the deal and to unlock higher profitability. Prysmian has now confirmed that six plants will be closed by Q1 2013 of which four are European operations where there is the greatest degree of overlap. Scheduled to close are metallic wire and cable plants at Derby, UK, Fercable, Spain, and Wuppertal, Germany as well as an optical cable facility in Livorno Ferraris, Italy. One high cost metallic cable plant in Asia will also be shut as well as an underperforming unit in China. Although some of the lost production will be transferred to other group factories, the single biggest effect will be felt in the UK with the exit of Prysmian from the low margin copper wiring drawing business. The Derby wire drawing and building wire plant has a capacity of 12kt, roughly 10% of UK rod consumption. **European brass mills also struggling** KME repo

rted a 15.5% year-on-year drop in its Q1 2012 sales to 114kt from 134.5kt a year ago.  Volumes grew in Germany, were stable in France, but fell in Spain and Italy.  The group attributed the poor outcome to weak construction activity and a steep decline in industrial manufacturing in the capital goods and consumer durables sectors.  Another aspect of the sales decline in Spain was the closure in 2011 of KME LOCSA, its flat rolled products manufacturing unit in Cordoba.  ASSOMET has also reported a 10% reduction in total Italian brass mill output to 156.2kt in Q1 2012 compared to 173.3kt a year earlier.  Earlier in the quarter, the Wieland Group revealed its results for FY2010/11, which ended September 30<sup>th</sup> 2011.  Sales dropped to 475kt compared to 477kt in the prior year, though profitability improved due to higher margins and a richer product mix.  Sales offices were opened in South Korea and Brazil last year while slitting centres are to be commissioned in India and South China during FY 2011/12. Commenting on recent market conditions the group statement said, “Since January there has been a slight recovery. Due to euro debt crisis, incoming orders from customers of the important markets continue to be on a low level: in Europe and Asia demand is declining.” 

### **Americas** 

**General Cable buys Alcan Cable** Only a month after writing about General Cable’s return to the US building market and an expansion in Brazil, there has been further corporate activity from the wire and cable maker.  The latest move is the $185m purchase of Alcan Cable from Rio Tinto in an all cash offer that is expected to close in the second half of this year, subject to regulatory approval.  Interestingly, Alcan Cable produces aluminium products, which will remind readers that Encore Wire is constructing an aluminium building wire factory.  These moves do point to further substitution pressures, which could dent copper demand in the years to come.  For now though tightness in the US aluminium rod market should prevent any major shifts away from copper. 

**Construction market appears to be recovering strongly** The re-entry into the building market of General Cable certainly points to confidence in the recovery of the US housing market and both hard data and anecdotes confirm this trend.  In fact, the US housing market seems to have been improving steadily since February 2011, with new private housing starts following an upward trajectory since then.  However, in November of last year there seemed to be an upward step change, which resulted in housing starts jumping from around 600kt per month to around 700kt where they now reside.  Even if the data just holds steady at this level for the rest of the year rather than continuing to make sequential month on month gains, this will still represent an increase of 15% on 2011 levels.  On the face of it, these factors all seem very positive for the US housing market, although an emerging trend that is less upbea

t is the fact that many of the new buildings seem to be smaller in size than those built prior to the financial crisis. Whether it be one less bathroom or a smaller overall square footage, our industry contacts report that this is tempering the benefit of the housing upturn. More worryingly for the longer term outlook is the fear that this puts future growth on a permanently lower trajectory if the trend of smaller houses were to continue. **Rod output falls back in April** After what appeared to be a strong upturn in rod output in March, the subsequent decline in April reminded us that one swallow does not make a summer. According to flash estimates from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics, April rod production fell by 9.1% year on year in April to 101.2kt and reversing the 8.1% gain of the prior month. Overall rod output for the first four months of this year is down by 0.4% on the January to April period of 2011 and perhaps belying the upbeat assessment of demand that rod producers have reported this year. It is curious that the AMBS rod data is not more up tempo as our discussions with rod mills point to firms being reasonably happy with their order intake. What is the bigger worry with respect to refined copper demand, however, is that the SDI La Farga rod mill is expected to come on stream in the second half of this year. This mill is to source all of its feed from scrap rather than cathode, with the worry that its output will grab market share from other players and therefore moderate the demand for refined cathode. **1% growth forecast for 2012 maintained** At the very start of the year, we did have discussions with clients on why our US consumption growth forecast of 1% was so low, given that the domestic market had started so well. At the time we remained cautious on the outlook and particularly for the second half given that we expected the SDI La Farga scrap mill mentioned above to take some market share and in doing so hit refined demand. Combined with the relatively sluggish actual data for rod output there seems to be very few reasons for us to change our forecast and therefore, we reiterate our 1% growth forecast for 2012. ### **China** **Government acts to boost economy** It is hard to say whether there was a specific data point that prompted the raft of measures aimed at shoring up Chinese economic activity or whether it was concern over what might come to pass. However, there were certainly a few negative releases to ponder upon over the past month or so, including the slowest rate of GDP growth si

nce the depths of the financial crisis, while IP growth for April also slipped back to lows last seen at the same time.  It was a cut in banks reserve requirement that came first, followed by rumours and then an official announcement of white goods purchase incentive schemes, which was then backed up by moves to bolster government investment spending.  Significantly, these measures should be supportive not only of economic activity in general but also of demand for copper. 

By now demand should be full steam ahead according to seasonal norms, although consumption in China continues to disappoint.  Order books of most semis producers remained at similar levels to April, although the decline in metals prices since mid-May encouraged some buying interest from fabricators.  Indeed, it is possible that fabricators might further increase their stocks in June following the decline in the copper price.  Wire rod production improved modestly from mid-May as orders for power cable for the power distribution grid came through, although there was only a little improvement in sheet and strip demand. 

**Schemes to boost white goods and investment** The State Council has announced a 26.5 billion yuan ($4.2 billion) scheme to subsidise the purchase of energy saving household electrical appliances for a one-year period.  Goods covered include air conditioners, flat-panel television sets, refrigerators, washing machines and water heaters that meet energy-saving standards.  Meanwhile, the government will allocate a further 2.2 billion yuan to subsidise energy-saving light bulbs and LEDs (light-emitting diodes) and 6 billion yuan to vehicles with engine sizes below 1.6 litres.  Another 1.6 billion yuan will be earmarked to promote the consumption of high energy-efficient motors.  The finer details of this subsidy programme will be issued in the middle of June and it is expected to be implemented in late June or July. Meanwhile, some major projects in the fields of railways, energy-saving and environmental protection, as well as infrastructure, educational and health care facilities in rural and western areas will also be encouraged, although this is likely to result in projects being brought forward rather than completely new ones announced.  Indeed, given the need for so called “shovel ready” projects then bringing forward plans makes the most sense.  However, there are no signs that the macro controls on the construction industry will loosen any time soon. 

**White goods sales poor so far this year** A closer look at the production data underscores the reason why subsidy schemes were announced, with output of appliances down almost across the board.  Air conditioners, the star performer last year with production growth of 26%, fell by 11.6% year on year in April and are down by nearly 7% in the year to date.  White goods are doing little better, with output of freezers and washing machines down so far this year, although

Auto production is the one sector that arguably did not need a subsidy, with output up by 3.4% in the first four months of 2012, although with the thrust of the incentives announced being on energy efficiency, perhaps it was felt necessary to also extend the offer to car drivers. **Investment to further lift electrical sector** Government spending on infrastructure was set to be a key driver for Chinese demand growth through 2012 even before the announcements outlined above. In the first quarter of this year, investment in the power industry rose by 3.6%, although this figure looks set to increase significantly based on projects being brought forward. This is already the largest end use sector and as such, strong growth in this largest sector will underpin Chinese demand. **Rod line to come on stream** In semis capacity news, Zhejiang Honglei’s new 150ktpa wire rod line started trial production in May. Output is said to be mainly focussed on internal magnet wire production. **Full year 7% forecast reiterated** The infrastructure and white goods announcements and their anticipated impact on demand have given us conviction in our full year forecast rather than leading us to increase it. We maintain our view of a recovery in the second half and reiterate our forecast of full year growth of 7% in refined copper consumption in 2012. A potential negative from the measures to boost economic activity is that they simply bring forward consumption, which clearly poses questions for demand growth next year. We still forecast growth in 2013 of 7.5% although the downside risks to this have clearly been raised somewhat. ### **SOUTH KOREA** **Semis data shows strong sequential recovery** South Korean production of copper and copper alloy semimanufactures has recovered from a poor start to the year. Output increased from 94.1kt in January to 101.3kt in February and then further to 107.3kt in March. Cumulative Q1 production now stands at 302.6kt only 2.3% behind comparative 2011 levels. However, within this total there is a big disparity between the trends in the refined copper intensive rod sector and the scrap intensive brass mill sector for copper and alloy rods, bars, tubes and sheets and strips. **Rod mills suffer in overseas markets** Korean rod mills

have enjoyed improving sales in the domestic market driven by a combination of rising local consumption of wire and cable and a rebound in wire and cable exports to the recovering markets of the Gulf States. However, overseas sales of rod have been hit by weak Chinese orders caused by tepid end use demand and the growing quantity and quality of rod from the new Chinese mills equipped with Southwire and Contirod continuous casting technology. In the Jan-April 2012 period, South Korean exports of rod, wire and stranded conductors dropped by 36% year-on-year to 20.7kt, compared to 32.4kt in the same period of 2011, and as much as 53.3kt in 2010. Over this three year timeframe South Korean exports to China and Hong Kong have tumbled from 32.6kt in 2010, to 15.6kt in 2011 and just 5.5kt in 2012. In consequence, Korean rod output dropped 9% year-on-year in Q1 2012 to 155.7kt versus 171.4kt in the prior year period. The main news in the rod business is Taewoo Metal’s decision to invest in a 120ktpa Southwire line. Last year it also raised its billet capacity to 50ktpa. Indonesian export ban** A ban on the export of unprocessed minerals from Indonesia came into force on May 6<sup>th</sup> . Under the new regulations, companies will only be allowed to continue exports of ores and unprocessed minerals by paying a new 20% export tax and by demonstrating to the government that they have plans to introduce downstream processing in Indonesia by 2014.  The principle exporters of copper concentrate from the country, PT Freeport Indonesia’s Grasberg mine and Newmont’s Batu Hijau operation are understood to be exempt from the export tax under the terms of their existing contracts of work.  However, these companies are still faced with the problem of how to deal with the proposed ban on concentrate exports from 2014.  Indonesia’s one existing copper smelter and refinery, Gresik (25% owned by PTFI), is capable of accepting ~1.1Mdmt/a of concentrates and with a refined metal production capability of ~300kt/a is forecast to be able to satisfy Indonesia’s domestic requirements until 2018.  Copper concentrate exports from Indonesia in 2012 are forecast to be ~1.0Mdmt rising to ~2.5M dmt by 2016 as head grades and production rates improve at Grasberg.  Aside from the practical difficulty of installing sufficient new smelting and refining capacity in such a short time frame, the economics of such an investment are also unfavourable, in our view.  With the capital investment for a 200kt/a smelter estimated to be in the region of $1.2bn and limited local markets for by-product sulphuric acid, a combined TCRC in the region of 50-60c/lb would be required to generate a reasonable financial return compared to our current long term forecast of 23c/lb. 

**Another smelter with arsenic processing capability experiences difficulty** While plans to re-open the La Oroya smelter in Peru remained stalled, the Namibian government instructed Namibia Custom Smelters (NCS) Tsumeb facility to reduce feed rates by half until projects scheduled for completion in the second half of the year and designed to capture fugitive emissions have been completed.  Like La Oroya, the Tsumeb facility includes a circuit to produce arsenic trioxide from dust recovered during the smelting process and can therefore accept concentrates with an elevated arsenic content.  Approximately half of the feed to the smelter, which produced 36kt of anode during 2011, comes from the

**Tintaya blockade** Xstrata is reported to be stockpiling concentrate production at its Tintaya mine in Peru due to blockades by locals and anti mining campaigners on the roads used to ship production to the port of Matarani.  The protests, ostensibly against alleged pollution of local rivers, are taking place at a time when Tintaya is facing demands to increase the local tax that it pays to the Espinar province where the mine is located.  The Tintaya mine, which supplied 74kt of copper in concentrate to the custom market during 2011, is due to be depleted later this year.  However, Xstrata’s production in the region is set to rise sharply in the coming years with the neighbouring Antapaccay mine (160kt/a) due to start ramping up production later this year.  It is also intended that the copper/molybdenum bulk concentrate produced at the 400kt/a Las Bambas project, scheduled to come on line in 2015, will be upgraded and filtered at the Antapaccay site. 

**Peruvian port investment** Consorcio Transportadora Callao (CTC), in which Trafigura subsidiary Impala Peru SA holds a majority 30% stake is reported to be investing $80M in new warehouse capacity at the port of Callao, close to the Peruvian capital Lima.  The facilities ,which are due to be completed by the end of 2013, will house copper concentrates from Chinalco’s Toromocho project which is scheduled to start ramping up to a production rate of 210kt/a of copper in concentrates in 2014.  CTC is engaged in a $230M project to upgrade the Callao port, which in addition to the warehouses will include new loading facilities and a hermetically sealed conveyor system. 

**Sandfire milestone** Sandfire Resources has yet to finalise sales agreements for copper concentrates from its 4kt/d plant at its Degrussa mine that is due for commissioning in the second half of 2012.  The company was, however, able to

announce a significant milestone in May with the first shipment of direct shipping ore (DSO) from the site. The consignment of 6.6k dmt at 30% copper has been shipped via Geraldton to customers in China. The high-grade DSO mined from the open pit will be sold under two sales contracts, with CWT and Yunnan Copper Corporation Ltd. ## Blister/anode and scrap markets **Chinese scrap imports also slow** With the continuing unfavourable arbitrage between the SHFE and LME markets and increased port side disassembly costs acting as a deterrent, reported Chinese scrap imports in April were 371kt, 14% lower than March and 2% lower than the same month in 2011 With demand from copper wire and brass rod mills weak due to poor order books, secondary smelters did, however, see improved availability of feed and local No.2 scrap spreads reversed their recent downward trend to trade in the range 3300 to 3500RMB/t (24 to 25c/lb) during May compared to 3200RMB/t (23c/lb) at the end of April. In Europe, lack of Chinese interest meant that scrap continued to be freely available during May. **New electronic scrap recycling capacity commissioned** First quarter production figures from Boliden included output from a new electronic scrap processing facility located at its Ronnskar smelter in northern Sweden. The SEK 1.3bn ($180M) investment, which has increased Ronnskar’s e-scrap recycling capacity from 45kt/a to 120kt/a, utilises a Kaldo furnace. This Furnace is a form of top blown rotary convertor suited to treating complex and potentially hazardous feed material as the vessel design allows different reaction steps to be executed in sequence whilst generating low off-gas flows. As the market for No.2 scrap becomes increasingly dominated by Chinese smelters, European producers are focussing increasingly on more complex feed materials such as electronic scrap.
